title: Remark
body_md:
We observe that fractional Fourier 
transforms are operators
that appear from the Weil representation 
of symplectic, or the metaplectic groups.
The Weil representation contains several
other types of operators. Common for
these operators are that they are
continuous on $\mathscr S (\mathbf R^{d})$ and
$\mathscr S '(\mathbf R^{d})$, and unitary on
$L^2(\mathbf R^{d})$ (see e.{\,}g.
\cite{CorGroNicRod,CorNic,dGo2,dGoLue,Ho1}
and the references therein.)

label: Def:GelfandTripple
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{Def:GelfandTripple}
Let
$\mathscr V _1,\mathscr V _2$ be
topological vector spaces
and $\mathcal H$ be a Hilbert space such that
$$
\mathscr V _1\hookrightarrow \mathcal H \hookrightarrow
\mathscr V _2.
$$
Then
$(\mathscr V _1,\mathcal H ,\mathscr V _2)$ is called a 
\emph{Gelfand triple}, if the following is
true:
\begin{itemize}
\item there is a hypo-continuous map
$(u,v)\mapsto (u,v)_{\mathcal H}$ from
$\mathscr V _2\times \mathscr V _1$
to $\mathbf C$ such that
$u\mapsto (u,v)_{\mathcal H}$ is linear
for every $v\in \mathscr V _1$ and
$v\mapsto (u,v)_{\mathcal H}$ is conjugate
linear for every $u\in \mathscr V _2$;

\vspace{0.1cm}

\item $\mathscr V _1$ is dense in $\mathcal H$;

\vspace{0.1cm}

\item if $u,v\in \mathcal V _1$, then
$(u,v)_{\mathcal H}$ is the scalar product
of $u$ and $v$ with respect to $\mathcal H$.
\end{itemize}
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
For the Gelfand triple in Definition 
\ref{Def:GelfandTripple} we observe the
following:
\begin{itemize}
\item
the map $(u,v)\mapsto 
(u,v)_{\mathcal H}$ from
$\mathscr V _1\times \mathscr V _1$ to $\mathbf C$ 
extends uniquely to a continuous
map from $\mathcal H\times \mathcal H$
to $\mathbf C$, and that this
extension agrees with the scalar product in
$\mathcal H$.

\vspace{0.1cm}

\item
$\mathscr V _2$ does not necessarily be
isomorphic with the dual $\mathscr V _1'$
of $\mathscr V _1$,
but is always continuously embedded 
in $\mathscr V _1'$, when using
the conjugate of the form
$(\, \cdot \,  ,\, \cdot \,  )_{\mathcal H}$.
\end{itemize}

label: Def:BFSpaces
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{Def:BFSpaces}
Let $\mathscr B$ be a solid QBF space of
order $r_0\in (0,1]$ on $\mathbf R^{d}$,
$C>0$ be the same as in 
\eqref{Eq:Solid},
and let $v_0\in \mathscr P _E(\mathbf R^{d})$
be submultiplicative.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The space $\mathscr B$
is called a
\emph{solid translation invariant
quasi-Banach function space on
$\mathbf R^{d}$} 
(with respect to $r_0$ and $v_0$), or 
\emph{invariant QBF space on $\mathbf R^{d}$},
if for any $x\in \mathbf R^{d}$ and
$f\in \mathscr B$, then $f(\, \cdot \,  -x)\in
\mathscr B$, and 
  
\begin{equation}\label{translmultprop1}
\Vert f(\, \cdot \,  -x)\Vert _{\mathscr B}
\le
Cv_0(x)\Vert f\Vert _{\mathscr B}\text ;
\end{equation}
  

\vspace{0.1cm}

\item The space $\mathscr B$
is called a \emph{solid translation 
invariant Banach function space on
$\mathbf R^{d}$} 
(with respect to $v_0$), or 
\emph{invariant BF space on $\mathbf R^{d}$},
if $\mathscr B$ is a Banach space and
an invariant QBF space on $\mathbf R^{d}$
with respect to $v_0$.

\vspace{0.1cm}

\item The space $\mathscr B$
is called a \emph{solid translation 
invariant normal quasi-Banach function 
space on $\mathbf R^{d}$} (with respect to $r_0$ and $v_0$), or 
\emph{a normal QBF space on $\mathbf R^{d}$},
if there is an invariant BF space
$\mathscr B _0$ on $\mathbf R^{d}$
with respect to $v_0^{r_0}$ such that
  
\begin{equation}
\label{Eq:NormQBFNorm}
\Vert f\Vert _{\mathscr B}
\equiv
\Vert \, |f|^{r_0}\, \Vert _{\mathscr B _0}^{1/r_0},
\quad
f\in \mathscr B .
\end{equation}
  
\end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
The assertion (1) follows from the fact that bounded sets remain bounded under continuous operations.

\par

Suppose that $\mathcal B$ is a quasi-Banach space of order $r>0$, and
let $T_1,T_2\in \mathscr I _\mathcal B$, $\{ f_j\} _{j\in \mathbf N}\in \operatorname{ON}$,
and
$\{ g_j\} _{j\in \mathbf N}\in \operatorname{ON}$. Then
  
\begin{align*}
\Vert  \{ ((T_1+T_2)f_j,g_j)\} _{j\in \mathbf N}\Vert _{\mathcal B}^r
&\le
\Vert  \{ (T_1f_j,g_j)\} _{j\in \mathbf N}\Vert _{\mathcal B}^r
+
\Vert  \{ (T_2f_j,g_j)\} _{j\in \mathbf N}\Vert _{\mathcal B}^r
\\[1ex]
&\le
\Vert T_1\Vert _{\mathscr I _\mathcal B}^r + \Vert T_2\Vert _{\mathscr I _\mathcal B}^r.
\end{align*}
  
By taking the supremum over all possible 
$\{ f_j\} _{j\in \mathbf N}\in \operatorname{ON}$
and
$\{ g_j\} _{j\in \mathbf N}\in \operatorname{ON}$ of the left-hand side, one obtains
$$
\Vert T_1+T_2\Vert _{\mathscr I _\mathcal B}^r
\le
\Vert T_1\Vert _{\mathscr I _\mathcal B}^r + \Vert T_2\Vert _{\mathscr I _\mathcal B}^r,
$$
which shows that $\mathscr I _\mathcal B$ is a quasi-normed space
of the same order as $\mathcal B$.

\par

We need to prove that $\mathscr I _\mathcal B$ is complete.
Suppose that $\{T_k \} _{k\in \mathbf N}$ is a Cauchy sequence
in $\mathscr I _\mathcal B$. Since $\mathcal B \hookrightarrow \ell ^\infty (\mathbf N)$,
it follows that $\mathscr I _\mathcal B \hookrightarrow \mathscr I _\infty$,
which in turn implies that $\{T_k \} _{k\in \mathbf N}$ is a Cauchy sequence
in $\mathscr I _\infty$, also. Since $\mathscr I _\infty$ is complete, there is a unique
$T\in \mathscr I _\infty$ such that
  
\begin{equation}
\label{Eq:OpNormLimit}
\lim _{k\to \infty} \Vert T_k-T\Vert _{\mathscr I _\infty}=0.
\end{equation}
  

\par

Now let $\{ f_j\} _{j\in \mathbf N}\operatorname{ON}$ and $\{ g_j\} _{j\in \mathbf N}\in \operatorname{ON}$
be fixed, and let
  
\begin{alignat*}{3}
\kappa &= \{\kappa (j)\} _{j\in \mathbf N} &
\quad &\text{and} & \quad
\kappa _k&= \{\kappa _k(j)\} _{j\in \mathbf N},
\intertext{where}
\kappa (j) &= (Tf_j,g_j)_{L^2} &
\quad &\text{and} & \quad
\kappa _{k}(j) &= (T_kf_j,g_j)_{L^2}.
\end{alignat*}
  
Then \eqref{Eq:OpNormLimit} shows that
  
\begin{equation}
\label{Eq:kappaLimit}
\lim _{k\to \infty} \kappa _k= \kappa ,
                                    
                                                                 
\end{equation}
  
with convergence in $\ell ^\infty (\mathbf N)$.
Since $T_k\in \mathscr I _\mathcal B$ and since $\mathcal B$
is a quasi-Banach space,
one has 
  
\begin{equation}
\label{Eq:AlternativeLimit}
\lim _{k\to \infty}
\Vert \kappa _k-\tilde \kappa \Vert _{\mathcal B}=0,
\end{equation}
  
for some $\tilde \kappa \in \mathcal B$, which depends on the choice of
$\{ f_j\} _{j\in \mathbf N},\{ g_j\} _{j\in \mathbf N}\in \operatorname{ON}$. Moreover,
since $\{T_k\}_{k \in \mathbb N}$ is a Cauchy sequence in $\mathscr I_\mathcal B$,
it follows that \eqref{Eq:AlternativeLimit} holds uniformly with
respect to $\{ f_j\} _{j\in \mathbf N}$ and $\{ g_j\} _{j\in \mathbf N}\in \operatorname{ON}$.

\par

A combination of \eqref{Eq:kappaLimit}, \eqref{Eq:AlternativeLimit},
and the fact that $\mathcal B \hookrightarrow \ell ^\infty (\mathbf N)$,
gives $\tilde \kappa = \kappa$, and since
\eqref{Eq:AlternativeLimit} holds uniformly with
respect to $\{ f_j\} _{j\in \mathbf N}$ and
$\{ g_j\} _{j\in \mathbf N}\in \operatorname{ON}$, one obtains
$$
\lim _{k\to \infty} \Vert T_k-T\Vert _{\mathscr I _\mathcal B}=0.
$$
This gives the result.

title: Proof
body_md:
Since \eqref{Eq:BargmannL2MapSympl}
is unitary, it suffices to prove that
$T_{\rho ,\theta}$ is unitary on
$A^2_\sigma (\mathbf C^{2d})$.

\par

Let
$$
A_j=e^{-i\rho _j\frac \pi 2}
\left (
\begin{matrix}
\alpha _{\theta _j} & \beta _{\theta _j}
\\
-\beta _{\theta _j} & \alpha _{\theta _j}
\end{matrix}
\right ),
\qquad
j=1,\dots ,d,
$$
which are $2\times 2$ rotation matrices.
Then it follows by straight-forward
computations that
  
\begin{align}
d\mu _{\sigma ,d}(z,w)
&=
d\mu _{\sigma ,1}(z_1,w_1)
\cdots
d\mu _{\sigma ,1}(z_d,w_d),
\notag
\intertext{and}
d\mu _{\sigma ,1}(A_j^{-1}(z_j,w_j))
&=
d\mu _{\sigma ,1}(z_j,w_j),
\qquad
j=1,\dots ,d,
\notag
\intertext{which give}
d\mu _{\sigma ,d}(A_{(\rho ,\theta)}^{-1}(z,w))
&=
d\mu _{\sigma ,d}(z,w).
\label{eq:GaussianMeasureRotationInvariant}
\end{align}
  
This, in turn, gives
  
\begin{align*}
\Vert T_{\rho ,\theta}F\Vert _{A^2_\sigma}^2
&=
\int _{\mathbf C^{2d}}
|F(A_{(\rho ,\theta )}(z,w))|^2
\, d\mu _{\sigma ,d}(z,w)
\\[1ex]
&=
\int _{\mathbf C^{2d}}
|F(z,w)|^2
\,
d\mu _{\sigma ,d}(A_{(\rho ,\theta )}^{-1}(z,w))
\\[1ex]
&=
\int _{\mathbf C^{2d}}
|F(z,w)|^2
\,
d\mu _{\sigma ,d}(z,w)
=
\Vert F\Vert _{A^2_\sigma}^2,
\qquad
F\in A^2_\sigma (\mathbf C^{2d}). \qedhere
\end{align*}

body_md:
\label{Thm:FracSymplFourTransf}
Let $\rho ,\theta \in \mathbf R^{d}$, and $K_\rho$
be given by \eqref{Eq:FracFourKernel}. Then
  
\begin{multline}
\label{Eq:FracSymplFourTransf}
K_{\sigma ,(\rho ,\theta )}(x,\xi ,y,\eta )
\\[1ex]
=
2^d\big (
K_{-\rho}(\sqrt 2\, x,\, \cdot \,  )
\otimes
K_{-\rho}(\sqrt 2\, \xi ,\, \cdot \,  )
\big )
(\sqrt 2\, A_{0,\theta}^*(y,\eta )).

label: Lemma:FracFourKernBargIdent
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof of (1) is only performed for
$\rho \in (\mathbf R\setminus 2\mathbf Z)^d$.
The other cases follows by straight-forward 
modifications and are left to the reader.

\par

The integrands in
\eqref{Eq:FracFourKernBargIdent}
and
\eqref{Eq:FracSymplFourKernBargIdent}
belong to $L^1(d\mu _d)$ and
$L^1(d\mu _{\sigma ,d})$, respectively.
Hence, if $f,g\in \mathscr S (\mathbf R^{d})$, then
  
\begin{align*}
(\mathscr F _{\rho}f,g)_{L^2}
&=
(\mathfrak V_d(\mathscr F _{\rho}f),
\mathfrak V_d g)_{A^2}
\\[1ex]
&=
\int \limits_{\mathbf C^{d}}
(\mathfrak V_df)(A_\rho ^0z)
\overline {(\mathfrak V_d g)(z)}\, d\mu _d(z)
\\[1ex]
&=
\pi ^{-\frac d2}
\int _{\mathbf C^{d}}
\left (
\int _{\mathbf R^{d}}
\mathfrak A_d(A_\rho ^0z,y)f(y)\, dy
\right )
\left (
\int _{\mathbf R^{d}}
\mathfrak A_d(\overline z,x)\overline {g(x)}\, dx\right )
d\mu _d(z)
\\[1ex]
&=
\iint _{\mathbf R^{2d}}K(x,y)f(y)\overline{g(x)}\, dxdy,
\intertext{where}
K(x,y)
&=
\pi ^{-\frac d2}
\int _{\mathbf C^{d}}
\mathfrak A_d(A_\rho ^0z,y)
\mathfrak A_d(\overline z,x)
d\mu _d(z).
\end{align*}
  
Evidently, $K$ is the kernel $K_\rho$ of
$\mathscr F _{\rho}$, giving \eqref{Eq:FracFourKernBargIdent}.
Therefore, (1) follows. In similar ways, one
deduces (2). The details are left to the
reader.

title: Proof
body_md:
The Bargmann transforms are
given by tensor products of one-dimensional
Bargmann transforms, and the matrix
\eqref{Eq:ArhothetaDef}
is a tensor product of $d$ $2\times 2$ matrices,
where each one acts on $2$ dimensional
phase spaces. This implies that
$K_{\sigma ,(\rho ,\theta)}$ is a
product of the same type of coordinate
kernels, given by \eqref{Eq:FracSymplFourTransfC}.
The result therefore follows if we verify
\eqref{Eq:FracSymplFourTransfC1Dim}, which is
the same as verifying the result for $d=1$.

\par

Therefore assume that $d=1$, and let
$$
x,y,\xi ,\eta ,\rho ,\theta \in \mathbf R,
\quad
\alpha =\alpha _{\rho,\theta}
\quad \text{and}\quad 
\beta =\beta _{\rho,\theta},
$$
be as in \eqref{Eq:AlphaBetaEuler}.
By Lemma \ref{Lemma:FracFourKernBargIdent}
(2) one has
                                     
                                  
  
\begin{align*}
&K_{\sigma ,(\rho ,\theta )}(x,\xi ,y,\eta )
\\[1ex]
&=
                                 
\frac 2\pi
\iint _{\mathbf C^{2}} 
\mathfrak A_{\sigma ,1}
(\alpha z+\beta w,-\beta z+\alpha w,y,\eta )
\mathfrak A_{\sigma ,1}(\overline z,\overline w,x,\xi )
\, d\mu _{\sigma ,1}(z,w).
\end{align*}
  
If $\gamma =e^{i\rho \frac \pi 2}$,
then the fact that
$\alpha ^2+\beta ^2=\gamma ^2$
gives
  
\begin{align}
&\mathfrak A_{\sigma ,1}
(\alpha z+\beta w,-\beta z+\alpha w,y,\eta )
\notag
\\[1ex]
&=
\exp \left (
-\big (
(\alpha z+\beta w)^2 +(-\beta z+\alpha w)^2 
+y^2+\eta ^2
\big )
+
\sqrt 8 \big ( (\alpha z+\beta w)y
+
(-\beta z+\alpha w)\eta \big )
\right )
\notag
\\[1ex]
&=
\exp \left (
-\gamma ^2\big (
z^2 +w^2 
\big )
-
(y^2+\eta ^2)
+
\sqrt 8 \gamma
\big ( (\alpha _\theta z+\beta _\theta w)y
+
(-\beta _\theta z+\alpha _\theta w)\eta \big )
\right )
\notag
\\[1ex]
&=
\exp \left (
-\gamma ^2\big (
z^2 +w^2 
\big )
-
(y^2+\eta ^2)
+
\sqrt 8  \big ( (\gamma z)
(\alpha _\theta y-\beta _\theta \eta )
+
(\gamma w)(\beta _\theta y+\alpha _\theta \eta )\big )
\right ).
\label{Eq:SympFracFourKernEval}
\end{align}
  
Since
$$
y^2+\eta ^2=(\alpha _\theta y-\beta _\theta \eta )^2
+
(\beta _\theta y+\alpha _\theta \eta )^2,
$$
it follows that the right-hand side 
of \eqref{Eq:SympFracFourKernEval}
        
                                        
                                              
is equal to
$$
\exp \left (
-\big (
(\gamma z)^2 +(\gamma w)^2 
\big )
-
(y_1^2+\eta _1^2)
+
\sqrt 8 \big ( (\gamma z)y_1
+
(\gamma w)\eta _1\big )
\right ),
$$
where
$$
y_1=\alpha _\theta y-\beta _\theta \eta
\quad \text{and}\quad
\eta _1
=
\beta _\theta y+\alpha _\theta \eta .
$$
By combining all these identities, it follows
that
  
\begin{equation}
\mathfrak A_{\sigma ,1}
(\alpha z+\beta w,-\beta z+\alpha w,y,\eta )
=
\mathfrak A_{\sigma ,1}
(\gamma z,\gamma w,y_1
,\eta _1 ).
\end{equation}
  

\par

If $c=\sqrt 2$, then a combination of
these identities with \eqref{Eq:BargSymplBargKernels}
gives
  
\begin{align*}
&K_{\sigma ,(\rho ,\theta )}(x,\xi ,y,\eta )
\\[1ex]
&=
                                    
\frac 2\pi
\iint _{\mathbf C^{2}} 
\mathfrak A_1(c\gamma z,cy_1)
\mathfrak A_1(c\gamma w,c\eta _1)
\mathfrak A_1(c\overline z,cx)
\mathfrak A_1(c\overline w,c\xi )
d\mu _{\sigma ,1}(z,w)
\\[1ex]
&=\left ( \frac 2\pi \right )^{\! 3}
H_1(x,y,\eta )H_2(\xi ,y,\eta ),
\intertext{where}
&H_1(x,y,\eta )
=
\int _{\mathbf C} 
\mathfrak A_1(c\gamma z,cy_1)
\mathfrak A_1(c\overline z,cx)
e^{-2|z|^2}\, d\lambda (z)
\intertext{and}
&H_2(\xi ,y,\eta )
=
\int _{\mathbf C} 
\mathfrak A_1(c\gamma w,c\eta _1)
\mathfrak A_1(c\overline w,c\xi )
e^{-2|w|^2}\, d\lambda (w).
\end{align*}
  

\par

By taking $cz=\sqrt 2z$ and $cw=\sqrt 2w$ as new variables of
integrations for $H_1$ and $H_2$, respectively, and using
\eqref{Eq:FracFourKernBargIdent}, we obtain
  
\begin{align*}
H_1(x,y,\eta )
&=
2^{-1}\int _{\mathbf C} 
\mathfrak A_1(\gamma z,cy_1)
\mathfrak A_1(\overline z,cx)
e^{-|z|^2}\, d\lambda (z)
\\[1ex]
&=
\frac {\pi ^{\frac 32}} 4
K_{-\rho }
(\sqrt 2\, x,\sqrt 2(\alpha _\theta y-\beta _\theta \eta )),
\intertext{and}
H_2(\xi ,y,\eta )
&=
2^{-1}\int _{\mathbf C} 
\mathfrak A_1(\gamma w,c\eta _1)
\mathfrak A_1(\overline w,c\xi )
e^{-|w|^2}\, d\lambda (w)
\\[1ex]
&=
\frac {\pi ^{\frac 32}} 4
K_{-\rho }
(\sqrt 2\, \xi ,
\sqrt 2(\beta _\theta y+\alpha _\theta \eta )).
\end{align*}
  
A combination of these identities gives
\eqref{Eq:FracSymplFourTransf}, and the
result follows.

label: Rem:FrSyFTLacksSympl
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{Rem:FrSyFTLacksSympl}
We recall that a $(2d)\times (2d)$ (real) matrix
$M$ is called symplectic (invariant)
if and only if
$$
\sigma (MX,MY) = \sigma (X,Y),
\qquad
X,Y\in \mathbf R^{2d}.
$$
Furthermore, suppose that
$T\in \mathcal L (\mathscr S (\mathbf R^{2d}),\mathscr S '(\mathbf R^{2d}))$ has kernel $K$. Then $T$
is called symplectic (invariant) if
$$
T(F(M\, \cdot \,  )) = (TF)(M\, \cdot \,  ),
$$
for every symplectic $(2d)\times (2d)$
matrix $M$. We observe that $T$ is symplectic
if and only if $K$ satisfies
$$
K(MX,MY)=K(X,Y),
$$
for every symplectic matrix $M$.

\par

The symplectic Fourier transform is symplectic 
invariant, because its kernel satisfies
$$
K_{\sigma ,(1,1)}(MX,MY)
=
\pi ^{-d}e^{2i\sigma (MX,MY)}
=
\pi ^{-d}e^{2i\sigma (X,Y)}
=
K_{\sigma ,(1,1)}(X,Y),
$$
for every symplectic matrix $M$. Similar
arguments show that any fractional
symplectic Fourier transform
$\mathscr F _{\sigma ,(\rho ,\theta )}$ are
symplectic invariant when
  
\begin{equation}
\label{Eq:ParameterIntegerChoices}
\rho ,\theta \in 2\mathbf Z
\quad \text{or}\quad
\rho ,\theta \in 2\mathbf Z +1.
\end{equation}
  
Furthermore, straight-forward evaluations
for other cases, show that these are the
only possibilities that fractional 
symplectic Fourier transforms are 
symplectic invariant.
Summing up, we have:
\\[2ex]
\emph{If $\rho ,\theta \in \mathbf R$, then
$\mathscr F _{\sigma ,(\rho ,\theta )}$ is
symplectic invariant, if and only if
\eqref{Eq:ParameterIntegerChoices} holds.}

title: Proof
body_md:
The equality \eqref{Eq:BargmannWigner} is a 
special case of \eqref{Eq:BargmannWignerAdv}.
Furthermore, since $\mathscr S (\mathbf R^{2d})$
is dense in $\mathscr S '(\mathbf R^{2d})$, and since
all involved mappings in 
\eqref{Eq:BargmannWignerAdv} are linear
and continuous, it suffices to prove
\eqref{Eq:BargmannWignerAdv} when
$F\in \mathscr S (\mathbf R^{2d})$.

\par

One has
  
\begin{align}
&(\mathfrak V _{\sigma ,d}(\mathscr W \! F))(z,w) \notag \\
&\qquad =
\pi ^{-d}
\iiint _{\mathbf R^{3d}}
\mathfrak A_{\sigma ,d}(z,w,y,\eta )F(y+\textstyle {\frac t2},y-\textstyle {\frac t2} )
e^{-i\langle t,\eta\rangle}\, dtdyd\eta
\notag
\\[1ex]
&\qquad =
\pi ^{-d}
\iint _{\mathbf R^{2d}}
\mathfrak A_{\sigma ,d}(z,w,y,0) I_1(w,t,y)F(y+\textstyle {\frac t2},
y-\textstyle {\frac t2} )\, dtdy ,
\label{Eq:IntExpr}
\end{align}
  
where
$$
I_1(w,t) = 
\int _{\mathbf R^{d}}
e^{-|\eta |^2+\sqrt 8\langle w,\eta\rangle -i\langle t,\eta\rangle}\, d\eta .
$$
By straight-forward computations, one obtains
$$
I_1(w,t) = \pi ^{\frac d2}
e^{2\langle w,w\rangle-i\sqrt 2 \langle w,t\rangle-\frac 14|t|^2}.
$$
Inserting this into \eqref{Eq:IntExpr} gives
$$
(\mathfrak V _{\sigma ,d}F)(z,w)
=
\pi ^{-\frac d2}
\iint _{\mathbf R^{2d}}
I_2(z,w,t,y)F(y+\textstyle {\frac t2},
y-\textstyle {\frac t2} )\, dtdy ,
$$
where
$$
I_2(z,w,t,y)
=
\exp
\left (
\langle w,w\rangle -\langle z,z\rangle +\sqrt 8\langle z,y\rangle -i\sqrt 2\langle w,t\rangle -(|y|^2+\frac 14|t|^2)
\right ).
$$
Taking $y-\frac t2$ and $y+\frac t2$ as new variables of integrations, we
obtain
$$
(\mathfrak V _{\sigma ,d}F)(z,w)
=
\pi ^{-\frac d2}
\iint _{\mathbf R^{2d}}
I_3(z,w,t,y)F(y,t)\, dtdy ,
$$
where
  
\begin{multline*}
I_3(z,w,t,y)
\\[1ex]
=
\exp
\left (
\langle w,w\rangle -\langle z,z\rangle +\sqrt 2\langle z,y+t\rangle -i\sqrt 2\langle w,y-t\rangle -\frac 12(|y|^2+|t|^2)
\right ).
\end{multline*}
  
If we let $z_1=z+iw$ and $z_2=z-iw$, this can be reformulated as
  
\begin{align*}
&I_3(z,w,t,y)
\\[1ex]
&=
\exp
\left (
-\frac 12(\langle z_1,z_1\rangle+\langle z_2,z_2\rangle +|t|^2+|y|^2) +\sqrt 2(\langle z_1,t\rangle +\langle z_2,y\rangle)
\right )
\\[1ex]
&=
\mathfrak A_{2d}(z_2,z_1,y,t)
  
                                           
=
\mathfrak A_{2d}(z-iw,z+iw,y,t).
\end{align*}
  
A combination of these identities gives
  
\begin{align*}
(\mathfrak V _{\sigma ,d}(\mathscr W \! F))(z,w)
&=
\pi ^{-\frac d2}
\iint _{\mathbf R^{2d}}
\mathfrak A_{2d}(z-iw,z+iw,y,t)
F(y,t)\, dtdy
\\[1ex]
&=
2^{-\frac d2}
\mathfrak V_{2d}F(z-iw,z+iw),
\end{align*}
  
which gives the result.

title: Proof
body_md:
We only present a proof for the result when $\rho _1=\cdots =\rho _d=\rho _0\in \mathbf R$,
leaving its modification into the general case to the reader.
Let
$$
\alpha =\alpha _{\rho ,\theta}
\quad \text{and}\quad
\beta =\beta _{\rho ,\theta}
$$
be as above.
   
                                                         
                      
                                                   
   
Then it follows from the definitions, Lemma
\ref{Lemma:BargmannWigner}, and \eqref{Eq:AlphaBetaEuler}
that
  
\begin{align*}
&\mathfrak V_{\sigma ,d}( \mathscr F _{\sigma ,(\rho ,\theta )}(\mathscr W \! F))(z,w)
=
(\mathfrak V_{\sigma ,d}(\mathscr W \! F))(\alpha  z+\beta  w ,
-\beta  z+\alpha  w )
\\[1ex]
&=
2^{-\frac d2}
\mathfrak V_{2d}F( 
\alpha  z  +\beta  w
-i(-\beta  z  +\alpha  w),
\alpha  z  +\beta  w+
i(-\beta  z  +\alpha  w))
\\[1ex]
&=
2^{-\frac d2}
\mathfrak V_{2d}F( 
(\alpha _{\rho ,\theta} +i\beta _{\rho ,\theta} )(z -iw),
(\alpha _{\rho ,\theta} -i\beta _{\rho ,\theta} )(z +iw)) 
\\[1ex]
&=
2^{-\frac d2}
\mathfrak V_{2d}F( 
e^{i(\rho +\theta )\frac \pi 2}(z -iw),
e^{i(\rho -\theta )\frac \pi 2}(z +iw)) 
\\[1ex]
&=
2^{-\frac d2}
\mathfrak V_{2d}(
\mathscr F _{(-\rho -\theta ,-\rho +\theta )}
F)(z-iw,z+iw)
\\[1ex]
&=
\mathfrak V_{\sigma ,d}
(\mathscr W \! (
\mathscr F _{(-\rho -\theta ,
-\rho +\theta )}F))(z,w).
\end{align*}
  
Hence
$$
\mathfrak V_{\sigma ,d}(\mathscr F _{\sigma ,(\rho ,\theta )}(\mathscr W \! F))(z,w)
=
\mathfrak V_{\sigma ,d}(\mathscr W \!
(\mathscr F _{(-\rho -\theta ,
-\rho +\theta )}F))(z,w).
$$
The result now follows from the fact that 
the symplectic Bargmann transform
is injective.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathfrak a \in s_{0,N}^w(\mathbf R^{2d})$ be given by
\eqref{Eq:FiniteRankSymb}. Then \eqref{Eq:FracSympAct}
shows that
$$
\mathscr F _{\sigma ,(\rho ,\theta)}\mathfrak a
=
\sum _{j=1}^N c_jW_{\mathscr F _{-\rho -\theta}f_j,\mathscr F _{\rho -\theta}g_j},
$$
and (1) follows from the fact that fractional Fourier transforms are
isometries on $L^2(\mathbf R^{d})$.

\par

As the partial fractional Fourier transforms are bijections on the family of orthonormal sets, by \eqref{Eq:FracSympAct}, this gives
  
\begin{align*}
\Omega _{\mathscr F_{\sigma ,(\rho ,\theta)}\mathfrak a}
&=
\{ \, \{ (\mathscr F_{\sigma ,(\rho ,\theta)}\mathfrak a ,W_{f_j,g_j})_{L^2} \} _{j\in \mathbf N}\, ;\, \{ f_j\} _{j\in \mathbf N},\{ g_j\} _{j\in \mathbf N}\in \operatorname{ON}\, \} 
\\[1ex]
&=
\{ \, \{ (\mathfrak a ,
\mathscr F_{\sigma ,(-\rho ,-\theta)}W_{f_j,g_j})_{L^2} \} _{j\in \mathbf N}\, ;\, \{ f_j\} _{j\in \mathbf N},\{ g_j\} _{j\in \mathbf N}\in \operatorname{ON}\, \} 
\\[1ex]
&=
\{ \, \{ (\mathfrak a ,
W_{\mathscr F _{\rho +\theta}f_j,
\mathscr F _{-\rho +\theta}g_j})_{L^2} \} _{j\in \mathbf N}\, ;\, \{ f_j\} _{j\in \mathbf N},\{ g_j\} _{j\in \mathbf N}\in \operatorname{ON}\, \} 
\\[1ex]
&=
\{ \, \{ (\mathfrak a ,
W_{f_j,g_j})_{L^2} \} _{j\in \mathbf N}\, ;\, \{ \mathscr F _{-\rho -\theta}f_j\} _{j\in \mathbf N},
\{ \mathscr F _{\rho -\theta}g_j\} _{j\in \mathbf N}\in \operatorname{ON}\, \} 
\\[1ex]
&=
\{ \, \{ (\mathfrak a ,
W_{f_j,g_j})_{L^2} \} _{j\in \mathbf N}\, ;\, \{ f_j\} _{j\in \mathbf N},
\{ g_j\} _{j\in \mathbf N}\in \operatorname{ON}\, \} 
\\[1ex]
&= \Omega _\mathfrak a ,
\end{align*}
  
and (2) follows.

\par

The assertions (3) and (4) now follow from (2) and straight-forward
computations. The details are left to the reader.

\label{Def:PointWiseInv}
Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbf C^{d}$ and $\mathcal B
\hookrightarrow \ell_0'(\mathbf{N}^{d})$ be a topological vector space.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mathcal B$ is called \emph{pointwize rotational invariant with
respect to $\Omega$}, or $\Omega$-invariant, if the map
\eqref{Eq:SeqSpRotInvariant} is a homeomorphism on $\mathcal B$,
for every $\varrho \in \Omega$.

\vspace{0.1cm}

\item $\mathcal B$ is called \emph{pointwize rotational semi-invariant with
respect to $\Omega$}, or $\Omega$-semi-invariant, if the map
\eqref{Eq:SeqSpRotInvariant} is continuous on $\mathcal B$,
for every $\varrho \in \Omega$.
\end{enumerate}

title: Remark
body_md:
In general, a solid QBF space $\mathscr B$ on
$\mathbf R^{2d}$ is not phase rotational invariant.
For example, suppose that $\mathscr B =L^{p,q}(\mathbf R^{2d})$ for some
$p,q\in (0,\infty ]$. Then $\mathscr B _\rho \neq \mathscr B$ when
$p\neq q$ and $\rho \notin 2\mathbf Z^{d}$.

\par

On the other hand, if $p=q$, then $\mathscr B _\rho = \mathscr B$
for every $\rho \in \mathbf R^{d}$. Consequently, $L^{p,p}(\mathbf R^{2d})=L^p(\mathbf R^{2d})$
is phase rotational invariant.

label: Thm:FracFourOnModSpaces
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Thm:FracFourOnModSpaces}
Let $\mathscr B$ be a solid QBF space on $\mathbf R^{2d}$,
$\mathscr B _\rho$ be as in
Definition \ref{Def:FrFTScales}, and let
$\omega ,\omega _\rho \in \mathscr P _A(\mathbf R^{2d})$ be such that
$\omega _\rho =\omega (A_\rho \, \cdot \,  )$, $\rho \in \mathbf R^{d}$. Then
$\mathscr F _\rho$ on $\mathcal H _{\flat _1}'(\mathbf R^{d})$ restricts to a
homeomorphism from $M(\omega ,\mathscr B )$ to
$M(\omega _\rho ,\mathscr B _\rho)$,
and
  
\begin{equation}
\label{Eq:FrFTModNorm}
\Vert \mathscr F _\rho f\Vert _{M(\omega _\rho ,\mathscr B _\rho )}
\asymp
\Vert f\Vert _{M(\omega ,\mathscr B )},
\qquad f\in \mathcal H _{\flat _1}'(\mathbf R^{d}),\ \rho \in \mathbf R^{d} .
\end{equation}
  
If, in addition, $\mathscr B$ is strict solid, then
\eqref{Eq:FrFTModNorm} holds with strict equality.
head: environment

label: Eq:FrFTonSTFT
title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to prove \eqref{Eq:FrFTModNorm}.
Let $\phi _0$ be as in \eqref{Eq:GaussWindow},
and let $f\in \mathcal H _{\flat _1}'(\mathbf R^{d})$.
By (1.35) in \cite{ToBhMa} and \eqref{Eq:FrFTScalesProp},
we obtain
  
\begin{equation}
\label{Eq:FrFTonSTFT}
|V_{\phi _0}(\mathscr F _\rho f)| = |V_{\phi _0} f(A_\rho \, \cdot \,  )| .
\end{equation}
  
This gives
$$
\Vert \mathscr F _\rho f\Vert _{M(\omega _\rho ,\mathscr B _\rho )}
=
\Vert V_\phi (\mathscr F _\rho f)\cdot \omega _\rho\Vert _{\mathscr B _\rho}
\asymp
\Vert V_\phi f(A_\rho \, \cdot \,  )\cdot \omega (A_\rho \, \cdot \,  )\Vert _{\mathscr B _\rho}
=
\Vert V_\phi f\cdot \omega\Vert _{\mathscr B},
$$
which gives \eqref{Eq:FrFTModNorm}. 
If, in addition, $\mathscr B$ is strict solid, then
the previous computations hold with equality at each step. This
implies that \eqref{Eq:FrFTModNorm} holds with equality, and the
result follows.

$M_\sigma (\omega ,\mathscr B )$ stays between $\Sigma _1(\mathbf R^{2d})$

only a rescaling of the ordinary Fourier transform, it follows that there
is a one-to-one correspondence between symplectic modulation
spaces and modulation spaces for such types of weight functions

\par

Consequently, in the common situations, symplectic modulation
spaces are merely a reformulation of the usual modulation spaces.
